justification: Every article provided concerns MYH2 as the fast type IIa myosin heavy chain gene causing dominant and recessive skeletal myosin myopathies (ophthalmoplegia, congenital contractures, muscle weakness, rimmed vacuoles), with no mention of Autism Spectrum Disorder in any study. No paper reports ASD probands, ASD cohorts, or autistic features segregating with MYH2 variants. The closest tangential mention is a single case report of a child with a motor developmental disorder and intellectual disability carrying MYH2 missense variants (PMID 30662633), and a WES diagnostic series including neurodevelopmental/neuromuscular genes (PMID 30009132), but neither assesses ASD, and intellectual disability alone is not a specific ASD precursor attributable to this gene. There is also no biological or pathway rationale presented linking fast skeletal muscle myosin to ASD neurobiology, so a Hypothesized rating is only weakly supported. The evidence therefore overwhelmingly supports a Novel relationship between MYH2 and ASD.

justification: None of the provided articles mention epilepsy, seizures, or any CNS paroxysmal phenotype. The entire literature set concerns CHRNA1 as the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α1 subunit at the neuromuscular junction, with variants causing congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia deformation sequence/multiple pterygium syndrome, pregnancy loss, and autoimmune myasthenia gravis susceptibility (PMIDs 29478601, 27748205, 29054425, 22482962, 22728938, 18567868). CHRNA1 is expressed at the neuromuscular junction rather than in neurons, so even a biological/pathway rationale for epilepsy is weak; the cholinergic receptor subunits implicated in epilepsy are neuronal, not this muscle subunit. A small amount of probability is retained for "Hypothesized" only because nicotinic cholinergic signaling is broadly relevant to excitability, but no article here supports that for CHRNA1 and seizures.

justification: Multiple independent human genetic studies report causal KCNC1 variants in epilepsy patients: the original exome study identified a recurrent de novo p.Arg320His in 11 unrelated PME probands plus 2 additional cases (PMID 25401298), a cohort of 20 MEAK patients with the same mutation was characterized clinically and electrophysiologically (PMID 28380698), novel de novo variants (p.Ala421Val, p.Cys208Tyr, p.Thr399Met) were found in five unrelated individuals with myoclonic/generalized epilepsy and developmental delay (PMID 31353862), and six unrelated patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy carried de novo p.Ala421Val (PMID 31353855). Familial segregation with maternal mosaicism further supports causality (PMID 29428275). Functional work shows dominant-negative loss of function consistent with disinhibition (PMIDs 29894724, 27629860). Irrelevant homonym/incidental mentions (opioid dependence GWAS, ADHD, Usher locus mapping) do not detract from this strongly replicated human evidence.

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 variants identified in autism patients; the only human genetic study (PMID 23326251) examined a multigene 5q31.2 microdeletion in a patient with developmental delay and then sequenced LRRTM2 in 330 ID/DD patients, explicitly finding no relevant alterations — a negative result, and for ID/DD rather than ASD. All other papers are molecular/cell-biological or animal studies showing LRRTM2 acts as a postsynaptic neurexin ligand organizing glutamatergic synapses (PMIDs 20519524, 30262834, 29784826, 30100184, 24005312), with autism cited only as background pathway context. Human variant findings in the set belong to NRXN1/NRXN2/NRXN3, not LRRTM2 (PMIDs 21424692, 31578233). The biology is directly relevant to the neurexin–neuroligin synaptic pathway implicated in ASD, so Hypothesized is the best fit, with a small allowance for Existing based on the deletion-region candidacy argument.

justification: The strongest human evidence is a single report (PMID 31300657) describing heterozygous de novo GRIA2 variants in 28 unrelated patients with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental abnormalities including ASD, supported by functional expression data showing loss of agonist-evoked current. This is compelling but comes from one publication; no second independent clinical cohort/family series in this list replicates GRIA2 variants in ASD probands. The only other human variant report (PMID 22669415) is a de novo deletion spanning both GLRB and GRIA2 in a patient with ID (not ASD), which cannot isolate GRIA2. Other articles are supportive background (GRIP1 variants altering GluA2 recycling in autism patients, PMID 21383172) or mechanistic/animal/in vitro work (Fragile X CP-AMPAR dysregulation, IQSEC2, neuroligin-3/VTA, Epac2, MeCP2), which bolster biological plausibility but are not GRIA2 variant evidence in humans. Therefore "Existing" best describes the current state, with residual probability for "Established" given the size of the single de novo cohort.

justification: PMID 31794024 reports original patient data: exome sequencing in three unrelated families (Caucasian, Turkish, French-Canadian) with seven affected children sharing a homozygous TRAPPC4 splice variant (c.454+3A>G), with early-onset seizures as a core feature, supported by SNP-array evidence against a shared haplotype and extensive functional validation (reduced TRAPPC4, TRAPP assembly defect, trafficking/autophagy defects, yeast model). PMID 32125366 is an independent report of the recurrent bi-allelic c.454+3A>G variant in patients with progressive encephalopathy, providing replication in additional probands (with a reply, PMID 32125358). PMID 32116085 is a commentary/mechanistic summary that supports biology but is not independent patient evidence. The remaining papers (PMID 20035503 on PDXK/Parkinson's, PMID 27052692 eQTL epistasis) are incidental co-mentions of TRAPPC4 unrelated to epilepsy. Residual probability for "Existing" reflects that the replication relies on a single recurrent variant and that the second report is available only as a title/letter.
